entries.title: ‘The Silent Art’
entries.summary: Kate Millett would never be more active or more in demand than she was in 1972. Two summers earlier, her debut book had made her a household name. entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
Kate Millett would never be more active or more in demand than she was in 1972. Two summers earlier, her debut book had made her a household name. Begun as her thesis for a literature Ph.D., Sexual Politics swelled into a wide-ranging examination of sex as a terrain of political contest and patriarchy as a ubiquitous force, adaptable but tenacious throughout history, structuring interpersonal life at every scale. The press seized on the book as an exemplary artifact of a new wave of feminism striking the shores of the mainstream.

After Time put her portrait on its cover and dubbed her “the Mao Tse-tung of Women’s Liberation,” Millett struggled to wrench the spotlight back toward the causes she’d been made to represent. She spoke at rallies, college auditoriums, and closed-door rap sessions. She appeared on Dick Cavett and on the steps of the New York capitol. In March 1972 she returned to Columbia, where she’d been a graduate student, to protest layoffs of custodial staff; in May she traveled to California to witness the trial of Angela Davis. And in April she mounted an art show called Terminal Piece.

Millett had been making art for over a decade, a parallel vocation that was met with mild curiosity when it was acknowledged at all. A spread in Life introduced her as a “furious young philosopher” before noting that she was also “a sometime artist” of “whimsical sculpture.” An accompanying photo shows her smiling broadly behind one of her creations: a cartoonish wooden bed with four oversized feet stretching out toward the camera. It was one of a suite of furniture pieces that brought Millett modest attention in the late 1960s, before the press reencountered her on the barricades. “Kate Millett’s sculptures all look alike and like Kate Millett,” Janet Malcolm wrote in The New Yorker. “They have a square-cut, blocky, strong, optimistic character.”

Terminal Piece was something else. No one would call it whimsical or optimistic. Millett’s installation has been restaged this summer at mumok, in Vienna, where it occupies its own shadowy room on the museum’s top floor. A wall of wooden bars cuts the space in two. Behind them are arranged two rows of folding chairs. A single mannequin sits off-center in the second row, her head bowed slightly, her right foot arched forward. She wears the loose navy dress of a prisoner, penitent, or sleeper, and incongruous black high heels. She may be waiting to stand and depart (terminal as in transit stop), or she may be waiting forever (terminal as in fatal).

It’s a disturbingly lonely work, especially from an artist who did not want for company. The 1972 opening at the Women’s Interart Center, a feminist gallery on 52nd Street in Manhattan, was packed with well-wishers. Writing in Ms., Millett’s friend Bertha Harris described the evening as a raucous party from which only the mannequin was excluded: “In the middle of our noise, she is a stillness like embalmed death.” Harris longed to free the woman from her cage, and as the night wore on some revelers finally did. Millett later remembered watching as her mannequin was swallowed by the crowd, “a rigid figure who could neither drink nor converse while they chattered and milled about.”

For months she had felt herself grow rigid, embalmed in her own celebrity. “I can’t be Kate Millett anymore,” she confessed in Flying (1974), a memoir of her effort to transcend her figurehead status. “It’s an object, a thing. A joke at cocktail parties.” When, she must have wondered, would someone liberate her?

It still surprises people to learn that Millett, who died in 2017, made sculptures, but a string of posthumous exhibitions has stoked new interest in them. Terminal Piece was previously revived at Bard College’s Hessel Museum in 2021. Later that year, the Dorsky at SUNY New Paltz mounted “Life After the Revolution,” a group show about the art colony run by Millett and her partner Sophie Keir on Millett’s Dutchess County farm beginning in the late 1970s. More attention was garnered by “Fantasy Furniture, 1967” at Salon 94 Design, which featured the furniture works made just before Millett was pushed onto the national stage.

Eerily animate, these pieces both invite and repel use. A 1967 photo shows Millett seated on Uncle Louis Stool with Boots, her back to the camera, her lower half obscured by the sculpture in a visual gag: its slender wooden legs are painted with striped stockings and wear oversized work shoes. Bachelor’s Apartment has a squat head made from a milliner’s hat block, blank but for a pair of wide blue eyes angled slightly to one side, puzzled and expectant. In place of its torso is a cupboard stocked with dishware; a wooden hand seems to hold one door open like a flasher’s trench coat.

Advertisement

For viewers who know Millett only as a firebrand, her furniture can be a revelation: clever and charming, but odd; in touch with the avant-gardes of its own moment, but as alive half a century later as it must have been when first shown in a basement gallery at Judson Memorial Church. Millett had lived in Japan at the start of the 1960s, where she fell in with a bohemian set of artists and poets more influenced by surrealism, Dada, and Duchamp than by the abstract expressionism that dominated in New York. Upon her return to the US, Millett—like many of her friends, including Yoko Ono and Carolee Schneemann—found an aesthetic home on the outskirts of Fluxus, a loose international movement that (in the words of its ringleader, George Maciunas) opposed “the separation of art and life.”

Much Fluxus work was self-consciously political. Maciunas imagined that by stripping art of its pretensions and exclusivity, Fluxus would “purge the world of bourgeois sickness.” Millett’s furniture was political, too, in the sense that Sexual Politics helped popularize: the sculptures concern “power-structured relationships” as they play out in the close quarters of home. Their ambivalently innocent and ominous tone speaks to the tenderness as well as the alienation of domestic life, its pleasures as well as its indignities. The two humanoid forms in Bed seem to stare vacantly at the ceiling. They aren’t touching; a break in the mattress ticking with which the piece is upholstered gives their double bed the look of twin beds pushed together, or coffins laid side by side. The conjoined chairs of Love Seat face in opposite directions, and the figures that occupy them likewise look past and away from each other.

Reviews of Salon 94 Design’s 2022 show tended to underline this incipient feminist critique while still describing the furniture as a buoyant relic of Millett’s not-yet-raised consciousness, a prologue to her activist career. That was, in fact, how Millett herself came to see it. In a 1988 essay for Art Papers, she wrote that her mid-Sixties sculptures were made “out of a happiness with form itself…intent upon ingenuity, a Mozartian wit and grace. I had a wonderful time.”

In her own telling, her approach changed overnight when, in 1966, she read a magazine article about the abuse and murder of an Indiana teenager named Sylvia Likens. Likens’s guardian enlisted her own children and neighbors in torturing the girl, who was confined to a basement for weeks before her death. The phrase I AM A PROSTITUTE AND PROUD OF IT was etched across her stomach.

Likens’s story struck Millett as “a devastation of the spirit like the collapse of a building.” It fueled the writing of Sexual Politics and gave her the image that defined her art for the next decade, including Terminal Piece: the cage. In the summer of 1967—the Summer of Love, for some—Millett spent six weeks constructing a maze of wooden walls and dowels in the basement of her Bowery building and filling it with dismembered mannequins. This installation, called Trap, was followed by the performance No, for which unsuspecting visitors were imprisoned within a structure Millett built inside Judson’s basement gallery. (The art critic Lil Picard, who was running late for a TV appearance, organized the crowd’s escape.) Situations, installed in 1968 at a community college in downtown Brooklyn, used Millett’s new motif to recast her earlier work. Pieces of furniture, now stripped of whimsy, were displayed in cages in the college’s courtyard: “the domestic safety of a dining room table” at once “exposed” and “enclosed in bars.”

Likens’s murder clearly had a profound effect on Millett; her 1979 book The Basement, which recounts the crime in horrible detail, attests to its enduring imprint on her thinking. But this conversion narrative neutralizes the bite of Millett’s furniture, some of which was made after she first read about Likens, and it threatens to clip the associative power of the work that followed. Even as the cage symbolized the extremity of women’s subjection, it also suggested links between misogyny and other kinds of “confinement,” as she wrote in Art Papers:

the torment of being someone’s amusement, someone’s job in that they are employed to torment you. Who are the food of guards and watchmen, their bland indifferent eyes. The captured, pawns of the state, of faceless government, disinterested army personnel, attendants of “corrections” or the “mental health system.”

Likens was “there in the shadows” of Trap alongside a row of urinals flanked by papier-mâché legs, meant to evoke US soldiers’ sexual exploitation of Vietnamese women. Perhaps Millett’s most infamous cage appeared in the 1970 People’s Flag Show at Judson, intended to challenge flag desecration laws that had been wielded against antiwar activists. Her contribution, The American Dream Goes to Pot, consisted of a toilet bowl detained in a wooden cell. The stars and stripes were draped over the bowl’s lip—to be flushed down the drain, presumably, though it always puts me in mind of some sewer creature crawling up through the pipes.

Advertisement

In this light the mannequin of Terminal Piece conjures what Millett called “the lone Giacometti-like stick of a citizen reduced to a number, a cell, a punch card, a clinical or criminal history.” While making it she read Solzhenitsyn on the Gulags and began to advocate for political prisoners; in subsequent months she would publish two long essays about Angela Davis in Ms. and teach a course on “Prisons and the Prison Movement.” At the same time, Terminal Piece is sparer and more ambiguous than its sibling works. It picks up their political concerns and knits them in turn to the artist’s inner turmoil, which was, in 1972, still mostly private.

To Janet Malcolm, whose New Yorker story published just weeks before Terminal Piece opened, Millett confessed her “puritanism about work” and the joylessness of her effort to keep art alive amid the media circus. Her husband Fumio Yoshimura, also a sculptor, told Malcolm that Sexual Politics “destroyed our quiet life.” Though their content was grim, her earlier cage pieces had channeled a certain hopefulness in both Fluxus and the women’s movement. By demanding their audiences’ active engagement, Trap and No took for granted that people can be moved to change their circumstances, and that art and ideas can spur that change. The inert mannequin of Terminal Piece may admit some disillusionment with that dream. In a short item in Parade, Millett said elliptically, “I feel an identification with the loneliness and despair of the figure because it’s a place I’ve been.” She had a history of depressions and would soon show signs of mania, for which she was hospitalized in 1973. The ordeal led her to see herself as one of “the underground people.” The asylum was part of the continuum of imprisonment that already preoccupied her work and defined her century.

Millett’s 1974 book Flying describes her struggle against celebrity and the fraying of her marriage, but it took her years to write about her time in institutions, just as it took years to write about Likens. In the meantime she made sculpture, which she once called “the silent art.” Her cages gave form to the prisons of fame, of psychiatry, of sex, and their “obdurate tangibility” provided a measure of relief from the vaporous meanings that clung to her.

Terminal Piece is too solid and too oblique to symbolize any one thing. At mumok, it anchors an ambitious show featuring dozens of artists across five of the museum’s floors, suggesting new links and associations. In lieu of biographical or historical through lines, the curators, Fatima Hellberg and Lukas Flygare, highlight the power dynamics that shape the act of looking itself: What does it mean to stand on the viewer’s side of the frame? On the artist’s? These questions helped me see that Terminal Piece is participatory in its own way. Millett’s mannequin might be an audience of one for the show that we make; as the exhibition program suggests, “It becomes unclear who exactly is being put on view.” (Millett once named Ionesco’s The Chairs and Beckett’s Waiting for Godot among her inspirations for the work.)

mumok’s galleries are full of obstructed sightlines and partial barriers to peek over or around. Mirrors, windows, and doorways recur, sometimes opening onto nothing. Many of the displayed artworks—like Kobby Adi’s The Machine (2026), in which a bioimaging device has been refitted to transmit live black-and-white footage to screens throughout the gallery—riff on surveillance and the conventions of documentary. Many appropriate mundane objects and make them strange. The show’s great discovery, for me, was probably Louis Goodman’s winning assemblages of forks, springs, jewelry, and other household odds and ends, from 1964—the same moment in which Millett was making her fantasy furniture.

And many of these artists share Millett’s interest in the intimate scale at which vast social forces mark our lives. In the years after Sexual Politics, as she strained to incorporate ever more causes into her feminism, she also worked to refocus it on what she described (quoting Thoreau) as “the quiet desperation” of the individual. This was evident in the writing for which she’s best known—the scholarly voice of her first book was soon supplanted by a nervy and vulnerable first person—and it was evident in sculptures like Terminal Piece. One thing the cage said to Millett was that each of us suffers alone. Yet she never stopped believing that suffering could be a basis for solidarity. There is a certain “responsibility these symbols confer upon us,” she wrote about her solitary sculptural figures in Art Papers. “There is no Sadean glorification of anguish at issue, no sentimental gloating over wretchedness—they are there to be liberated.”

entries.title: Jerry Survives
entries.summary: As an artist in the second half of the twentieth century, Jerry Moriarty did everything you weren’t supposed to do: he painted people, he painted places, and, perhaps worst of all, he told stories with pictures. It’s important to note how not-accepted this was between the 1950s and 1970s, in the messy aftermath of abstract […]
entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
As an artist in the second half of the twentieth century, Jerry Moriarty did everything you weren’t supposed to do: he painted people, he painted places, and, perhaps worst of all, he told stories with pictures. It’s important to note how not-accepted this was between the 1950s and 1970s, in the messy aftermath of abstract expressionism, when many artists had disowned figuration and family in favor of non-objective paint-spattered flats. But Jerry drew pictures of America as Americans remembered it, if not even still lived it: childhood, parents, home. Like many of his peers, he spent much of his career alone in a small Manhattan studio but, upon retirement, he moved back to his childhood home.

Like many people, I was first introduced to Jerry’s work in the pages of Art Spiegelman and Françoise Mouly’s RAW magazine via his strip Jack Survives, in which the eponymous character, both Jerry’s dad yet also not his dad, passed quick, quiet moments of the everyday. Jerry’s bold, solid, black-and-white strips seemed to have been pencilled by Ernie Bushmiller and inked by Edward Hopper, proffering a loud-but-soft view of middle-class midcentury America. Like so much in RAW, it felt strange, but unlike so much in RAW, it also felt strangely familiar. Jerry’s strips somehow caught the scent of sun-warmed houses and 1940s sofas and made the time when men wore hats and women wore housedresses feel real. A window into what I’d imagined my grandparents’ early lives might’ve been like, his work chided the squareness of that generation but with a gentle empathy for their difficulties (war, economic scrimping), without the dismissiveness that some baby-boomer writers and artists seemed to have for their parents. His bold, sturdily composed panels and solid sense of objects and people lent it an eternal quality, seemingly in conflict with the ineffability of its domestic situations and the dissipating half-life of conversations, thoughts,

and the words one says only when talking to oneself, the whole adding up to not exactly a comic strip, but something like a picture-poem with a punchline.

The first collection of Jack Survives, published in 1984 by RAW Books and Graphics, was designed by Spiegelman and Mouly, its cover separating Jerry’s eight-crayon-box colors and his bold black brush drawing into two layers, the ink lines printed on an acetate jacket which under one’s fingers slipped in and out of alignment with the bright hues below. It reminded me of the anatomy overlays in my grandparents’ encyclopedias, and offered a lesson in not only how comics were printed but also the basic cognitive distinction between drawing and painting (to say nothing of the difference between remembering something and actually seeing it). His original comics pages are strange palimpsests, in which penciled memory-details disappear under acrylic white or emerge as emphasized ink, the approach more evident in the 2008 reprint of Jack Survives, in which Jerry chose to highlight his pages’ simultaneous boldness and delicacy in full-color scans instead of the contrasting black-and-white of the first edition. In a way, this echoed his overall artistic method: Jerry’s assertive, Hopper-esque drawings—see Hopper’s etchings, especially—mellowed once they made it into his paintings, softening into full-color acrylic studies on paper before ending with his almost diaphanous oils on canvas. These paintings, generally composed of three, sometimes four brightly colored panels, were meant to be not just looked at, but read.

Jerry wanted to be accessible and eschewed pretension, later labeling himself a “paintoonist” as a sort of self-effacing and disarming pre-strike against anyone who might consider denigrating his efforts, for which he was always on high alert. In his early life he’d tried abstraction and also working as an illustrator, but found he was comfortable with neither, disappearing into a private life subsidized by working as a teacher at the School of Visual Arts in New York. Over a period of several decades he produced a considerable oeuvre that basically no one ever saw unless they visited his Manhattan studio/loft.

As I tried to become a thoughtful cartoonist myself, Jack Survives was never far from my mind, frequently open on my drawing table at moments of desperation, where I’d reread his strips several dozen times while avoiding my own. Eventually, I got to meet Jerry in person, the first time at a 2004 exhibit of his paintings in Manhattan which Spiegelman had organized. I’d thoroughly expected to shake the hand of a dour, literary Thornton Wilder in a houndstooth jacket and trim tie, but instead was met by a spritely, energetic marionette in bright orange pants who seemed to leap between his canvases, weightless long white hair trailing a beat behind him as he narrated the backstory to each one, the paintings’ fictional characters melding with his experience of making them.

Advertisement

At that point in his career he’d been drawing and painting “Sally,” a character who was a sort of authorial stand-in (again, partly him yet really not him) and about whom he spoke from the inside (“Sally wanted to climb the tree”) and the outside (“I felt so wrong painting that”)—and, most importantly, with real affection. None of the paintings were for sale. He made his work only for himself, amassing it slowly and, as he later described it to me, working in the “art protection business” to make sure that nothing ever escaped, except the very few pieces he offered as gifts. Neither a gallery-affiliated fine artist nor a job-hungry commercial artist, he had more or less committed career suicide, leaving such possible-life husks behind so he could float above them, living purely through, and for, his work.

The second time I met Jerry was at a party in 2007 at Spiegelman and Mouly’s apartment, with other RAW cartoonists in attendance, Kim Deitch and Charles Burns and Gary Panter among many more. I ended up talking to Jerry alone for what must’ve been almost an hour, he at one point going into great detail about how he lived off a whole pre-cooked grocery store chicken and six chocolate chip cookies per week, carefully apportioning them over seven days to keep himself and his cat alive. He offered this not as a look-at-me-I’m-crazy detail but as what we’d now call a “life hack.” During this hour in his presence a very tangible sense of aloneness enveloped me. I mention this not to embarrass his memory, but to clarify: as Jerry said in an interview I did with him for The Believer in 2009, “I am a loner, and I fully understand why that makes me strange to society … but I am not lonely. Being alone is total freedom for me.”

Put another way, his memories were his company. This is indeed just the sort of person who would discover his childhood home was for sale, buy it, and move back in. There, he set up his studio in the very basement where he’d made art as a kid and where his dad would arrive home from work to sit and talk with him as he drew and painted. Now in his seventies, Jerry started drawing and painting images of his father and his mother at the ages they were when he was a child, but with himself pictured as the old man he had become. In one painting, Jerry’s head peeps through a rip in the paper ceiling above his father, who sits in an easy chair below; in another, old Jerry sits at the kitchen table talking to his young mother, easily half his age. (My stepfather, now living alone following the death of my mother in May, told me that every night he sits in his armchair and tells her what’s happened over the course of the day.) These were the people and memories that meant the most to Jerry—his parents, his siblings, his childhood dog. (When he was a kid, his dog had been taken away by the humane society, a loss for which Jerry offers a painted corrective: the dog returns to the front door, where a child-sized old-man Jerry lets him in, then spends the night on the floor, cradling him.)

These are not the traditional tropes of comics, but of literature and poetry. My favorites of Jerry’s works get at those moments when we completely surrender, when we’re at our most vulnerable—exactly the opposite of what comics’ brash denigration and guffaws generally paper over. His tenderness, when it’s the focus, is without precedent in cartooning—or, for that matter, in much contemporary art. And that Jerry managed it all within such a “loud,” disreputable language as comics is especially remarkable. He was the first cartoonist to realize that by leaning into the loud, like his cartoonist hero Bushmiller, one might be able to more closely approach the quiet of real life. It’s one of the mysteries of comics, hiding somewhere between the giant/infinitesimal horror of a childhood fever and the lyrical dissonance of the bebop jazz that Jerry loved (and played).*

Advertisement

Jerry thought and drew (though what’s the difference?) a lot about death. It is the implicit theme in his late work Whatsa Paintoonist?—which is also one of the weirdest titles for one of the greatest graphic novels ever. This is the book that collects his imagined revisitations with his parents, painted in the home where they all once lived, and in which, through his drawings, Jerry says his goodbyes to them. It is also the home where, in March of this year, Jerry’s nephew found him dead. The book resuscitates the childhood feeling that most of us spend our lives tamping down and dismissing, if not completely extinguishing. It’s a magical, alchemical experience of reading and seeing, somehow mixing Jerry’s own memories of childhood and parents with one’s own, on the page and in the mind’s eye. It reawakens some sleeping small self within us, completely disarmingly and without pretension. It captures the feeling of life, but most especially, of love.

entries.title: The Profiler
entries.summary: It seems as though Rachel Syme has interviewed all the grandes dames of New York and Los Angeles. She drank cosmopolitans with Carol Burnett, accompanied Sarah Jessica Parker to the ballet, shopped at Rachel Comey with Parker Posey, gabbed with Patti LuPone over Skype, and gabbed with Barbra Streisand on a landline. At a time […]
entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
In “The Art of the Interview,” season four of the podcast The Critic and Her Publics, Merve Emre speaks with top writers and journalists to discuss the subtle skill of conducting an interview. The Review is collaborating with Lit Hub to publish transcripts and recordings of each episode.

It seems as though Rachel Syme has interviewed all the grandes dames of New York and Los Angeles. She drank cosmopolitans with Carol Burnett, accompanied Sarah Jessica Parker to the ballet, shopped at Rachel Comey with Parker Posey, gabbed with Patti LuPone over Skype, and gabbed with Barbra Streisand on a landline. At a time when the glossy magazine profile seems hopelessly compromised, Syme uses her deep knowledge of musicals, fashion, and old Hollywood to add substance to what could be breezy brushes with fame and fortune. And she loves a good yarn. Our conversation is full of behind-the-scenes stories, which show how the interview can transform a mere celebrity into an idol.

Merve Emre: Most of the people in our audience are college students. How did you get from where they are to where you are today?

Rachel Syme: I grew up in Albuquerque, New Mexico. I always wanted to get to New York. I went to Stanford in California and didn’t have designs on being a writer, I just knew that I wanted to do something in New York with publishing. I was a big reader, and I wrote, but I didn’t really know that journalism was something I could do. I came to New York in the mid-2000s and did the Columbia Publishing Course, where you could specialize in magazines or books, and people would come and talk to you about how to break into these worlds. I was on the magazine track, and we had people come speak to us from Conde Nast and New York and Time Out New York.

I went to all the big magazines, dropped off my résumé, and asked for informational interviews with whoever would see me, like Anne Hathaway in The Devil Wears Prada. My first job, which I got by doing just that, was an unpaid internship at New York magazine. I did that “job” for six to eight months, then I moved into fact-checking and wrote some short features, and got started on an editorial career. I went to work at a few start-up magazines, and then I went to work for Tina Brown at The Daily Beast.

While I was in editorial, I realized I wanted to write. In 2008, the worst time ever to try to be a freelance writer, I gave myself a run at it. I said, “If I can get a byline in The New York Times and in The New Yorker by the end of the year, then I’ll keep doing this.” At the very end of that year, I got both, which was crazy. Then I was a freelance writer for eleven years. It was a wild time, and I was getting bigger and bigger assignments, but also bigger and bigger rejections. Ultimately, The New Yorker gave me a little trial where I would do “On and Off the Avenue,” which was the fashion column that had been running since the 1920s. That column grew, and I became a staff writer at The New Yorker in 2020. I was doing a lot of interviews. What I was known for, and what I still do, are celebrity profiles.

I was at a lunch recently with a celebrity profiler who was intensely cynical about the celebrity profile. Particularly today, when everyone is so media trained, and when all these new media platforms make it possible for anything anyone says to be taken out of context, screenshotted, and circulated.

Yes, it also makes it possible for them to just completely tell their own story. Why would they want to have it mediated by someone else?

Right. So talk to me about being a celebrity profiler at a time when that subgenre of the interview seems hopelessly compromised.

It is compromised. The genre has changed dramatically from when I started, and even more dramatically from the glory days. Everybody wants to go back to the 1950s, when you could just spend a year with Marlon Brando, travel with him on the road and sleep inside his bathroom, and get everything. That’s just not going to be a thing that exists anymore. The juice isn’t worth the squeeze. Especially, as you said, when there are so many venues for having things taken out of context and misrepresented. There’s a sense of fear that most people have around these processes, and it has gotten so much harder to book bigger ingenues.

I’m in a really lucky position at The New Yorker because there’s a certain kind of person that still wants to do this work. When I first go to a subject and tell them what it’s going to require, their publicists have a heart attack. “It’s going to take a year, and you have to spend this amount of time with them, and I can’t be there?” There’s so much hand-holding, telling your subject, “It’s going to be okay.” You’re like, “Here are the people who’ve had a New Yorker profile: Isadora Duncan, Obama, Barbra Streisand. You could be in this illustrious company.” It’s definitely a hard sell, and it doesn’t always work.

Advertisement

I also have my own qualms with it as a form. As things change, as you get less access, people are doing a lot more viral stuff. If I only get one shot at this and it has to go big on all these platforms right away, then I have to push this person into territory very quickly that hasn’t been built on trust. So I think that the whole enterprise is getting rejiggered and reimagined, but I don’t think it’s dead.

I don’t think it’s dead either. It occurred to me that your type of subject is a kind of person who’s maybe later in their career, a little more secure, with a deep artistic repertoire behind them. Someone who is willing to embark on this journey with you. Is that a fair description?

Yes, I have a definite type: eccentric older woman of the arts who has lived a long life as a broad and who’s still alive to tell you about it. They have so much experience, and you can wrap their life in that history, as opposed to somebody who’s just starting out. If Stephen Sondheim’s I’m Still Here was embodied in a person, that would be my ideal subject.

What do you want from those people? I’m curious what it is that you glean from them.

Selfishly, I’m always going into every interview trying to get somebody to teach me how to live, or how to be an artistic person of integrity, a person who has longevity. These are the things that I’m looking for answers to in my own life. Sometimes I think I have the nosiest job in the world; I just get to ask people how they did it. In certain ways, it’s self-serving for wisdom’s purpose. But I also just love stories. I love a person who has yarns and wants to go on at length about something, even if it might sound obscure or eccentric. I let people have a lot of rope because ultimately there’s something they’re trying to get at the end, and I want to unravel it. So for me, it’s an adventure, and it’s a bigger adventure with people who’ve lived longer lives. There’s a lot more to unspool.

When someone hasn’t bought the hard sell, why do you think that is? How do you get people to trust you?

It’s different from subject to subject. I often offer a first conversation, off the record. But it’s not so they can tell me all of their secrets and then I’ll keep them safe. It’s so they can meet me and I can meet them. I also try to let them know I have an extensive knowledge of their work, and that I’m not coming to this subject lightly. I’m not trying to get the same profile everyone else is getting. I have to have a unique pitch. You don’t want to present as a fan, but you do want to present as a person who is a student of what they’re up to, and it helps if you have a point of view. But you also have to let your point of view change as you meet someone, or else there’s no reason for you to be there.

Who is the subject you’ve profiled where your preconceptions changed most dramatically over the course of reporting and writing the piece?

In many different ways, they’ve all thwarted or exceeded my expectations. Sarah Jessica Parker was an interesting one because I went in understanding that she was a perfectionist and an exquisite physical comedian. But when you watch her work, everything seems so effortless, so light and bubbly, full of a charismatic effervescence that her seriousness and absolute commitment to her performance surprised me: trying on dresses for eighteen hours a day, arriving hours early to mark out all her props. Every cigarette she ever smoked on Sex and City had been practiced beforehand.

In terms of personalities, there are people that I went to thinking they’d be really forthcoming, and they weren’t. Or people that I thought were a little bit tragic, and they turned out to be unwilling to pity themselves.

After the off-the-record conversation, how do you build trust over the course of six months or a year of visiting people at their homes, on set, watching what they’re doing?

Advertisement

It’s a different process for everyone. Some people feel comfortable right away. I’ve had subjects where I get there for the off-the-record lunch, and halfway through they go, “You can turn that on. We can start.” But in general what I like to do first is the basic groundwork. Let’s talk about your childhood. Let’s go through the major career highlights, brick by brick. You get those out of the way, so that you have the scaffolding of their life. But you’re also showing them you’ve done your research, and showing you have a handle on the material, which is a good way to build trust. So many famous people are interviewed by somebody who didn’t do the research. If you can come to them with a sense of complete reverence for their work and also some obscure stuff that you dug up from the 1980s—like, “I remember when you were in a tarot card phase, and you went on this weird show”—then they can really get into it. They don’t have to just skate on the surface, like with everyone else. As much as you’d like to go into it cold, you also have to read everything they’ve ever done, read every interview they’ve ever given, and then try to forget it, because it also has to feel naturalistic. I like my interviews to just feel like gabbing.

It’s similar to the way I prepare to interview a literary figure. I have a real allergy to a person who begins to tell a scripted story, especially one I’ve encountered in multiple other interviews. I think, Right, these are your talking points. I imagine this is more common and more intense with more famous celebrities. I’m curious how you deal with a moment where you feel like you’re getting the talking point or you’re running into media training.

With celebrities, you’re always going to run into media training. You have to let them get through that part because it’s protective for them, and it’s the narrative they’ve spun for a reason. Sometimes it’s to deflect, sometimes it’s to self-aggrandize. But you can actually glean something from the canned lines they’re telling you. For example, the legendary comic actress Carol Burnett tells the same story in her memoir and on talk shows all the time. She returns to the same bullet points about her life, and it was really hard to get her to push past that. Then you realize that there’s a certain narrative of the plucky girl that made it that she wanted to maintain, and that it has great romance for her. In some ways, that profile became about a person who has a narrative they are spinning about their life that’s often overly sunny and positive in relation to what they actually went through as a child. That’s an interesting contrast. So you have to find little ways to catch them off guard. If they say something that they’ve said a thousand times before, you can say, “Yeah, I’ve heard you say that. But….” They know that you’ve caught them in the moment of trying to spiel.

You have a wonderful moment where you do that in the SJP profile. You guys are going to the ballet together, and she is gushing over your outfit.

This became the one part of the profile that later, SJP, who I am still in touch with, was like, “I remembered it differently than you.” We were meeting at the ballet, where she is on the board, and it was the opening night of a new show. I thought, “We’re going to Tatiana, this great restaurant in Lincoln Center, and then we’re going to go to the ballet. I’m going with Carrie Bradshaw. I must wear a fit, right?” So I came in this strapless blue cocktail dress with a choker. And then she showed up in an old, men’s button-up shirt, halfway tucked into jeans with a hat. In the piece I say something like she’s so embedded in New York culture that an opening night at the ballet is just another Tuesday for her. But when we got there, she was very into telling me that she loved my outfit because she didn’t want me to feel uncomfortable. She just kept saying, “Don’t you look so great?” and then she turned to this group of women having dinner in fur coats and says “Ladies, doesn’t she look pretty for the ballet.” It was this moment where I was like, I understand what you’re doing: You can’t not be on the charm offensive at all times and make other people feel like you’re there for them. But there is an authentic part of her personality that’s so kind and solicitous.

That same night when we went into the auditorium and she saw that she had amazing seats, she said, “These are amazing seats they gave me.” And I was like, “You’re on the board. You’re like the number one spokesperson for the New York City Ballet.” But she’s still so wowed by New York, and charmed by it all, that it wins you over. But you have to step back from it and see it as an interchange that we’re having, where you present it as it happened.

My sense is that when most people interact with famous people, they are much more solicitous than they would be with anybody else. Fame has this way of making other people want to be in your good graces. I imagine there are many profilers who can’t quite maintain the distance between wanting the famous person to like them and being able to carve out enough space to report on something objectively.

Yeah, it’s difficult. And when you spend so much time with someone, you do start to wonder, where’s the line here? Are we friends? But you have to remember that you’re both doing your jobs, and your job is to tell the story, to accurately get at the artistry, and to talk about what makes them interesting and viable as a cultural figure. That’s been the mission of the profile since The New Yorker coined the term. So you have to be able to step back and have a little bit of distance. But it’s difficult because fame is intoxicating, and really famous people seem to occupy a very different world. They smell better. They have glossier hair. They just seem to be in a cloud. There’s just some beautiful lavender aura around them, where the whole pH of the room changes. When you’re around somebody like that, it’s very hard to have any objectivity.

What about famous people who do seem more like us? Your profile of Natasha Lyonne, for instance, is stripped of the aura of celebrity in a way that neither the Burnett nor the SJP profile are.

Lyonne was a really interesting subject because she was so game, basically saying, Come with me to everything. Come inside my inner sanctum. Lyonne was really open to the process and has been misinterpreted so much over the course of her life. When we were doing our profile, she was in the process of discovering herself as a director. In the second season of Russian Doll, she was the sole showrunner and had just started a new production company. She was thinking about writing and directing a lot more. So what looked like a profile was really about the making of a director, not the life of a formerly troubled actress. She was open to the idea of me watching her as she ascended to this next level. The thing about Lyonne that’s so refreshing is that she doesn’t have a filter, not in the way that so many people do. She’s very famous, but she also doesn’t give a shit about being press trained. She’s been through worse than a quote being misunderstood, and she was a lot more open to the process because of that. I find a lot of people are also open to the process when they have reverence for profiles they’ve read of other celebrities. It’s very difficult to draw people out who have never read The New Yorker and don’t know what it’s about.

Thinking about your type—the type of subject to which you can bring your deep knowledge of film and fashion and various forms of middlebrow culture—I was wondering if you feel like your type is dying out, given the way that the whole constitution of celebrity has been changing over the past twenty years?

I see some young people that I think are poised to be very interesting older women, that have an eccentricity and a point of view. But yes, I think my type is going extinct. It’s a sad feeling, especially when you’re thinking about the type that would be excited about the opportunity to sit at length and talk about their work. Back when magazines were the only game in town, doing a profile indicated to somebody that their work mattered, that it was worth a reporter sitting for hours to have them talk about themselves—and the currency being exchanged was attention. But now, you can get attention in so many different places. If anything, they’re being trained to think of profiles as deeply intrusive, an opportunity for somebody to betray you or misunderstand you, rather than a chance to have someone look into why you do what you do. What’s dying out is an attitude more than the people.

So how do we get that back?

Well, the question is, do we need to? I always feel like if something’s dying, you can try to keep it alive against all odds, or you can also evolve along with the world. You have to figure out what you value and what you want to do. I wonder what your take is on profiles and what you think their usefulness is in this current environment.

I have a great love of the profile with the absent subject at its center, like Gay Talese writing “Frank Sinatra Has A Cold” for Esquire or anyone who’s ever tried to profile Elena Ferrante and has to write around her.

Or my profile of Lady Gaga because we had only forty minutes together and it was the craziest day of my life.

Why was it the craziest day of your life?

It was a cover story during A Star Is Born. I went to her studio, which used to be Frank Zappa’s house. Already, I’m going into this very kooky, magical, mystical place that has secret passages and trees of life painted on the wall. In her Star Is Born era, she was very into this Marilyn Monroe, high heels, platinum blonde look, and so she shows up looking like a 1950s movie star, and takes me to the living room, which has a twenty-foot picture of her own face from the end of A Star Is Born. It was like a phantasmagoria of the movie. Then she takes me down to the basement studio into a room that has great acoustics and starts belting “Shallow” at me, a capella. Then she took me to the studio and played me the soundtrack, and we used that as a road map for the interview, talking about each song then pushing on different aspects of her career, but she wouldn’t really talk about more than the music, so I was having to look for the words under the words. That was a ride around because she’s sort of a shapeshifter who doesn’t have allegiance to anyone. I like the ones with the absent center, that can be really fun. Those are definitely much more about the writer and not the person.

Do you really think that’s true? It’s like people who say all criticism is autobiographical. I understand why that’s such an appealing thing to say and believe, but I’m not sure I believe that it’s true.

Now that you’re pushing back on it, I may have misspoke. They’re not all about the writer. You’re obviously working in service of the material. I have a hot and cold relationship with profiles that are about the writer. There’s some that I really have come to love where it’s about this person’s meta experience of writing the profile, and how they came out on the other side of the reporting experience as a changed person. Every time Janet Malcolm wrote about somebody, it was like, Where am I? One of my favorite Malcolm profiles of all time is of the fashion designer Eileen Fisher. She goes to her house and notices that Fisher’s cat is out and lives under the deck, and she just keeps repeating, “I kept wondering if the cat was okay.” This has no relevance to anything, but Malcolm’s hand-wringing about the cat’s mental health is just so revealing there.

I’m writing an introduction to a new edition of In the Freud Archives, so I’ve been thinking a lot about Malcolm and about the historical changes in the profile over time. She was sued for libel over a New Yorker profile, but part of what brought that lawsuit was something that profilers at The New Yorker used to do all the time, which was to have seven or eight separate meetings with a subject and then compose everything to make it look like the person held forth for hours and hours over a single meal. So the whole form of the profile has really shifted over time. It used to be the way that you impress yourself onto it was by doing these wonderful stylistic tricks.

That is, to be honest, why many of my favorites are from an earlier time, because they blurred the line between fact and fiction. The vibes were realer, in a strange way. You’re always hearing these stories about reporters that didn’t take notes but remembered everything the person said. I believe it about one person alone, Robert Caro, who apparently can remember a quote verbatim three days later. But, other than that, I think you were just making up stuff that sounded right to you. At the same time, a lot of these celebrities felt very seen by these things and didn’t have problems with them. Now, every single quote is fact-checked, which is a good thing legally, but also entails a very different attitude. The celebrity has all of this protection from you.

I think writers themselves increasingly appear in profiles because what they can do behind the scenes, how they can make their presence felt in the actual form of the profile, is increasingly constrained.

I agree. More and more that’s the only kind of profile you can write. I’m not in my pieces that often, but when I am, it’s because there’s no other way to get things across. I profiled the fashion designer Thom Browne, and he is incredibly specific about what everybody wears at his workplace. He calls it “uniform,” where you have to wear full Thom Browne. You get $10,000 worth of it when you start and have to wear it every single day you work there. He had his first couture show in Paris, and the invitation said, “Please wear gray,” which I took to mean “Please wear Thom Browne.” But I don’t have Thom Browne, and I wasn’t about to borrow it from my subject. So I went to Galerie Lafayette in Paris the day before the show and ran up to the Thom Browne section, and there was a jacket that was on deep sale, and I almost bought it. As I was walking up to buy it, I was like, “I don’t want to spend 800 euros.” I just can’t do it. I’m trying to please this person at his fashion show. What’s the point? I already had a gray Rick Owens dress that I’ve had for a million years, so I just wore that. I came to the show, and the first thing his publicist said was, “You’re in gray. Oh my God, thank you.” And the first thing Thom said to me was, “You’re in gray.” I had to put that in the piece because of the rigidity of the way he makes you feel, this anxiety around not being in the gang. There was also a time I went to the Thom Browne store and tried on everything, and it wasn’t for me. Not because I don’t love it aesthetically, but I just couldn’t find anything that felt right. We really struggled whether or not to put a passage in the piece about my experience of being in the clothes, and we realized that that was probably a little too much of me.

I’m of two minds about the writer putting themselves in. Some editors really don’t like it because they feel like it’s lazy and don’t want a chronicle of you becoming this person’s best friend. The other way to look at it is that it’s not a story of a person, it’s a story of an encounter, and that encounter has two people. Your experience with a subject is as valid as their quotes and biography.

One of the guests for this season of the podcast is Orna Guralnik, the Couples Therapy therapist. Everything you’re saying is making me look back on the episodes we’ve recorded and realize that another title for this whole season could have been “Couples Therapy,” or “The Couple,” because every single person we’ve spoken to has said something similar: you’re always offering up a double profile, a double interview, a double exposure, and the task of the person doing the interviewing is figure out the right balance between the two people that are being put on display.

I sometimes think if there’s a chance to make myself look embarrassing in a piece, I’ll take it, because I owe this person a tiny bit of my own self-exposure, as they’re giving me so much.

Who do you feel like you’ve given the most of yourself to, whether it appeared in the final piece or not?

The person I’m profiling right now, who will be revealed in September when the piece comes out, is so interested in my own life. He makes me talk about myself a lot more than I would prefer, but I think that’s his style. I’m trying very hard not to give into that, because I think it’s a self-protective thing. I also talked about myself a lot with Burnett, and one of the reasons that happened was because she’s someone I just wanted to tell about my life. Every single person has a different calibration for how much you’re going to share, how much they’re interested in you. I’ve had subjects who are not interested in me at all, and there are other people who, before they’ll ever really trust me, need me to give.

Does it wound you if people to see you as a non-person, or do you think that’s just the nature of the transaction?

No. I understand how transactional this work is. I hate that word because it sounds very cynical, but I do understand they have a reason for saying yes. But you don’t want it to feel too impersonal, otherwise you feel like you’re not getting anything real, ever. You want to have a real conversation, and that can never happen between two people until you see each other as two people.

entries.title: The Road to the Rent Freeze
entries.summary: On the evening of June 25, minutes after New York City’s Rent Guidelines Board voted to freeze the rent for a million rent-stabilized apartments across the five boroughs, I caught up with a tenant I know named Josie Wells. Standing outside the auditorium in East Harlem where the vote had just occurred, we spoke about […]
entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
On the evening of June 25, minutes after New York City’s Rent Guidelines Board voted to freeze the rent for a million rent-stabilized apartments across the five boroughs, I caught up with a tenant I know named Josie Wells. Standing outside the auditorium in East Harlem where the vote had just occurred, we spoke about the implications of the freeze for her own apartment, which she rented from the real-estate group Pinnacle until the company filed for bankruptcy and put over five thousand of its units—including her own—up for auction. After Pinnacle filed, Josie helped build the Union of Pinnacle Tenants, which has continued to organize even as a new landlord has taken over some properties.

“I don’t know if it’s gonna change my life,” she told me, a paper kazoo in one hand and a slice of pizza in another. “My rent is so high, there’s utilities, food prices,” she went on. “So, yeah, it’s huge, it’s huge, it’s huge…and it’s just a breather.” After weeks of speaking with tenants in rent-stabilized units across the city, I had heard enough to recognize her measured debrief not as critique but as agitation toward what else might be possible for a tenant movement adjusting to formal power, under a mayor who has promised “a city we can afford.”

The day before the vote, I met Mrs. Liu on a bench across from a skate park outside her building in Chinatown. Since 2004 Mrs. Liu has been a member of CAAAV: Organizing Asian Communities, an organization of working-class Asian immigrants in Manhattan and western Queens, which co-chaired this year’s rent freeze campaign. She has lived in this twenty-unit building since 1996, when she moved to the neighborhood and started work at a garment factory; it has been sold to new owners six or seven times since she and her family arrived.

She took me up to her apartment, which has two small bedrooms and not a lot of natural light. Five family members share the cramped space, sleeping on small cots. The kitchen is also the living room, and the kitchen sink is also the bathroom sink. Laundry hangs to dry in the corner, between a stack of tupperware and a shelf with pill bottles and collagen peptide powder. In a tank on a small table where they eat, the family keeps six koi fish as pets. Above the table Mrs. Liu maintains a small shrine featuring two framed Buddhist images, candles, and fresh apples. A postcard from Niagara Falls is pasted on the wall over the door.

Mrs. Liu’s rent is already frozen, thanks to a program called the Senior Citizen Rent Increase Exemption (SCRIE), which allows applications from tenants sixty-two and over with a household income under $50,000. Even so, this year she attended the Rent Guidelines Board’s hearings in Manhattan and testified, as she has every year since 2011, as part of the citywide effort to freeze the rent for all stabilized tenants. “It’s for the young ones… People of the past helped us, and now it’s our turn,” she told me. “I see young people, even gentrifiers in the neighborhood, struggling…. They’re working, but it’s not easy for them.”

“So often we’ve discussed politics as if it is an intellectual debate,” Mayor Zohran Mamdani said this past April at an event marking his first hundred days in office. “And for working people, there is very little time for that kind of a debate. Working people want to know: what will you deliver? How will you make it easier to afford rent on the first of the month?”

On the campaign trail, as I wrote in these pages last summer, Mamdani found his way alongside working-class tenants with whom he had already been collaborating for years: in addition to universal child care and free buses, the rent freeze became one of the three central components of his affordability agenda. Those tenants, through organizations like CAAAV, meanwhile, had spent those years sharpening their analysis of how the real-estate industry drives returns to investors at the expense of the nearly 70 percent of New Yorkers who rent their homes. They resolved that they needed a mayor who would champion those who lived on the wrong side of these profit motives, and they came to see organized tenants as a potential electoral bloc that could make it happen.

When Mamdani shocked the Democratic establishment in the primary and then handily defeated the disgraced former governor Andrew Cuomo in November, that bet started paying off. But there’s campaigning and then there’s governing. Delivering a rent freeze wasn’t going to be straightforward.

The rent can only be frozen by a vote of the Rent Guidelines Board (RGB), an independent body that, once appointed by the mayor, can technically decide whatever it wants. To maintain a balance, two spots are reserved for tenant representatives and two for owner representatives, with the remaining five for “public” representatives who are required to have at least five years of experience in finance, economics, or housing. In one of his first viral campaign videos, Mamdani, noting that eight of Mayor Eric Adams’s nine appointees to the board had finished their terms, promised to replace them with representatives “who understand that landlords are doing just fine.”

Advertisement

In the months that followed, that claim would be hotly contested. New York’s landlords have pushed for steady rent hikes, insisting that, without them, owners would not make enough money to keep up with building maintenance. Earlier this year in Phenomenal World, J.W. Mason, a John Jay College economics professor, analyzed landlords’ monthly average gross income and operating costs and found that this assertion was mostly wrong: the “great majority” of residential properties make much more than landlords spend on them. Between 2021 and 2024 landlords’ net operating incomes rose by 30 percent. (For the small minority of buildings where this is not the case, Mayor Mamdani has proposed a city-backed insurance fund to combat soaring premiums and promoted a state hardship program for capital expenses.)

There is indeed a crisis brewing in the political economy of housing, both in New York and across the country—but as Mason and others have argued, it has less to do with straight-up operating costs and more to do with debt. Landlords are overleveraged, many having gambled with Covid-era low interest loans, borrowing to finance the rehabilitation of their current properties and the acquisition of new ones. Now, years on, they are struggling to pay those loans back under very different economic conditions, leading to what the researchers Ruthy Gourevitch and Jacob Udell have assessed as “escalating financial distress” in the multifamily rental market. Nationwide, as Gourevitch and Udell wrote in a policy brief in November, loan delinquencies “have nearly doubled in just the last year,” recently reaching their highest rate in a decade.

If New York City building owners might not do “just fine” under the rent freeze, in other words, it is generally not because their buildings cost too much to run but because, per Mason, “they borrowed too much to buy buildings at inflated prices, based on an expectation that rents would rise faster than they actually did.” Their gamble only made sense, and their deals only “penciled,” because they believed they could rely on passing ever-increasing burdens to their tenants. But tenants are already squeezed, and they can hardly be expected to mitigate the risks embedded in their landlords’ business models. The bind facing overleveraged owners is real—but it is not for tenants to solve.

Adams oversaw rent increases every year, for a cumulative increase of more than 12 percent during his time in office, and as his term came to an end he worked to entrench the RGB responsible for those hikes. On December 18, 2025, with two weeks left in office, he announced four appointments and reappointments: a finance professor, a landlord attorney, and a Merrill Lynch executive, plus one tenant lawyer.

Still not sworn in, Mamdani was undeterred. “We will use all the tools at our disposal to deliver [the rent freeze],” his team said in a statement, “and last-minute appointments do not change these facts.” Sumathy Kumar, executive director of the New York State Tenant Bloc, a coalition of tenant organizations throughout the state, shared the mayor’s certitude: “We are getting our rent freeze.”

In the end Adams’s last-ditch attempts to scuttle Mamdani’s plans failed, seemingly not due to any illicit pressure campaign but due to the strength of the electoral mandate: few board appointees, it turned out, wanted to be on the wrong side of the popular incoming administration. Twelve hours before Adams was set to leave office, the Merrill Lynch executive—who might have been a crucial vote against the freeze—withdrew. Adams tried to replace him, but the replacement declined the appointment. Once Mamdani was sworn in, he got to make six appointments to the board.

But that was still no guarantee. The mayor’s role was done, and in the following months the administration proceeded with caution to avoid breaking rules that prohibit it from interfering with the work of the independent agency. But City Hall did take the opportunity to launch a flagship civic education experiment. On April 29, flanked by Tascha Van Auken, the commissioner for the Mayor’s Office of Mass Engagement, and Cea Weaver, director of the Mayor’s Office to Protect Tenants, Mamdani announced Organize NYC, a project of Van Auken’s office, which aimed to bring “the people-powered movement that elected Mayor Mamdani to the work of governance.” It would start by hosting trainings across the city to inform tenants of their rights and about the RGB process. (I was a presenter at the Chinatown and Harlem events, sharing a basic history of the tenant movement in New York.) He described it as a way to “keep New Yorkers involved in the work of shaping the future of our city.” Hundreds turned up to these evening gatherings in May, mostly held in high school cafeterias. They left with invitations to knock doors with OME to get people out to the RGB’s annual hearings, which had been scheduled for Queens, the Bronx, Manhattan, and Brooklyn throughout June.

Advertisement

At the same time, organizers outside City Hall turned the RGB hearings into ever more energetic theaters for the tenant struggle, holding rallies and packing the rooms with tenants ready to testify in favor of the freeze. Their efforts more than doubled engagement from previous years; by the date of the final vote the coalition’s members—among them CAAAV, CASA, the Met Council, Housing Organizers for People Empowerment (HOPE), and the New York City Democratic Socialists of America—had organized around 330 testimonies at the hearings and submitted some 700 written and audio statements.

The landlords fought back. Kenny Burgos, CEO of the New York Apartment Association—a group that convenes owners and managers of some 500,000 rent-stabilized apartments—had at one point played basketball and smoked hookah with the mayor when they were colleagues in the state assembly. Now he made the rounds on local news and social media, presenting himself as a contrast to Mamdani, repeating the arguments about maintenance costs and peddling anti-freeze hyperbole: “We are on a path to destroy the housing people live in,” he told Curbed. At the Brooklyn RGB hearing, a pro-landlord group called the Gotham Housing Alliance bussed in paid actors dressed as zombies—with raggedy clothes and fake blood—to symbolize the regulated units that, the landlords argued, would be reduced to empty “zombies” if the owners couldn’t afford to maintain them.

The day of the final vote proceeded in dramatic fashion. Just hours before the tenants and board members gathered at El Museo del Barrio in Harlem, Christina Smyth, the landlord attorney Adams had reappointed, resigned from the board, effective immediately, in protest of what she characterized as an illegitimate process. In a three-page letter posted to her LinkedIn, she accused the board of ignoring its own data and made her final case against the freeze, again citing the oft-repeated though imprecise argument about maintenance costs:

Please understand me when I tell you that a freeze does not help the people it claims to protect. It does not lower the cost of running a building. It does not pay for a boiler or a roof or an elevator. It widens the gap between what a building costs to operate and what it is allowed to collect… When these buildings fail, it is not the people who cast these votes who pay the price… It is the family in the building no one is maintaining. They are the ones with the most to lose, and they are the ones I am most worried about.

Smyth’s argument called back to the central debate between the freeze’s supporters and detractors over who ought to bear responsibility for the causes of systemic failure. (In a lawsuit filed in late July, a group of landlords cited her resignation, alleging that the Mamdani-appointed board “made a mockery of its statutory mandate” and had succumbed to political pressure. And yet even the one member of the board who voted against the freeze said during a recent public appearance that he “observed no interference by the administration in individual members’ decisions.”)

From the auditorium stage at the museum, after a few other points of business, the RGB’s chair, Chantella Mitchell, called a vote on the main item: a zero-percent increase for one-year-leases and the city’s first-ever freeze for two-year leases. Five of the members voted in favor before Mitchell turned to Maksim Wynn, the remaining owner representative on the board. Instead of providing an immediate response, he launched into prepared remarks. The audience was raucous—leading chant after chant, completely drowning out Wynn’s commentary, which nevertheless continued for over five minutes. Finally tenants up front shushed the crowd as they realized Wynn was coming to an interesting conclusion, arguing that, with rents too high for people to afford, and rent collection low as a result, a rent freeze was actually in the owners’ interest:

There is a subset of the rent-stabilized stock that is in real distress, but the underlying causes are systemic ones. Those systemic issues need to be addressed, but at this moment the tools this board has are more likely to cause harm to owners rather than help, while the tools that the city and state have will definitively help…. At this moment in time, with the city taking the first steps towards the capital and expense interventions owners need, and the imminent risk of cratering economic occupancy, a zero percent increase on one- and two-year leases is in owners’ best interests.

The crowd quieted just enough to hear his vote, which secured the freeze, and then erupted once more. I sat next to a tenant named Magda, a member of CASA, a Bronx organization that had co-chaired the rent freeze campaign with CAAAV. She wore sunglasses throughout the proceedings, chatting to me about how anxious she was about the rent. When she heard the final count, she jumped to her feet, whipped off her glasses, and FaceTimed a friend, exclaiming with joy. Tenants filed out of the auditorium to the party on the plaza outside the museum, which expanded onto the sidewalk and toward the park across the street and then to a bar a few blocks away. Organizers played “We Are The Champions” from wheeled speakers as Josie, Mrs. Liu, Magda, and hundreds of other tenants celebrated.

When I asked her what got the freeze done this time, Kumar from the Tenant Bloc was straightforward. “This happened because of organized tenants,” she said. “The RGB process always felt like a sham, with board members looking at their phones while tenants poured their hearts out…and two years ago we decided to do things differently.” She was referring to the bloc’s decision to prioritize the mayoral election as an intervention into the rote annual hearings. “We decided to elect a mayor committed to a freeze, and he appointed a board that actually listened to tenants.”

Mamdani’s politics, which are not just his but those of the movement that shaped him, insist that it is possible to deliver a city we can afford, and more. Breathing room is not nothing; it’s a precondition for what comes next. This is a movement built on challenging not just the high cost of rent but the very notion that tenants’ homes are treated as a vehicle for owners’ money-making. It should come as no surprise, then, that the organizers’ eyes were already trained to further points on the horizon: a rent rollback, a statewide expansion of rent stabilization, and—as a way to address the crisis of overleverage—municipal or tenant buyouts of distressed properties.

Joanne Grell—a rent-stabilized tenant in the Bronx and, like Magda, a member of CASA—grabbed a mic, addressing the group gathered around her during the celebration. She echoed Josie: “New York, I hope you can breathe tonight.” Then her remarks turned to what the movement could do next, from taking over buildings to securing universal rent control. “A rent freeze,” she said, “is not the end of our story. It’s proof of what’s possible… Who here believes that anything is possible?” Hands shot up throughout the crowd.
